extracted.intended_audience: readers of The Spectator / literate early-18th-century London public
extracted.subtask_description: Short essays and observations on theatre, acting, playwriting, social character-types, and manners published in a periodical (The Spectator). Includes criticism, examples, and prescriptive remarks about performance and social behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural representation in acting
rubrics_metrics.description: Praise for actors who "represent nature excellently" and avoid the common fault of "doing too much." (Text: "There is certainly nature excellently represented in his manner of action; in which he ever avoided that general fault in players, of doing too much.")
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Cave Underhill admired for natural, restrained comic acting, especially in 'still-life' characters (stiff, heavy, stupid). Colley Cibber's comments describe Underhill's face and fixedness as strengths for such roles. Anti-pattern: overacting or excessive embellishment that departs from natural behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overacting / economy of gesture
rubrics_metrics.description: Actors should not 'do too much' — effectiveness comes from restraint and truth to character rather than excessive action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scoring note: performances that convey character through controlled, appropriate expression and timing are superior. Underhill's success as a gravedigger illustrates that minimal, precise choices can produce comic effect where exaggerated action would fail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality in tragedy / avoid formulaic plot
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique that many tragedies follow the same design so closely that "from the beginning of the first scene, the frequenters of the house may know, as well as the author, when the battle is to be fought, the lady to yield, and the hero to proceed to his wedding and coronation."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: strive for novelty and unpredictability in plot and dramatic turns. Anti-pattern: recycling stock plot-structure and predictable beats across five acts. The author expresses impatience with mechanical tragedies and a desire for fresh material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid reliance on ready-made rhetorical stock (similes/lines)
rubrics_metrics.description: Satirical remark that the author has "the farewell of a general... the principles of a politician... all my oaths ready, and my similes want nothing but application," implying the problem of plugging in ready-made rhetoric.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: dramatic speeches and rhetorical passages should feel earned and specific to the situation, not pasted from a commonplace book. Anti-pattern: using generic, pre-fabricated sentiments that render speeches clichéd.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actor fidelity to the author's text (not adding to authors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation that some players do not "add to his authors; for the actors were so dull in the last age, that many of them have gone out of the world, without having ever spoke one word of their own in the theatre."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: the passage both notes historical actors who did not improvise and contrasts them with later practice. Guidance: either faithful delivery of the written text or judicious, character-consistent additions may be valued; the text praises those who stick to natural representation rather than needless interpolation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character archetype: 'Very Pretty Fellow' (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Definition and criteria for a 'Very Pretty Fellow': one exalted above others by peculiar sprightliness, distinguishing vigour, jaunty behaviour, admitted everywhere, whose very errors and absurdities contribute to his success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Colonel Brunett (fashionable by will), three drinking brothers (Hogshead, Culverin, Musket), and other named exemplars. Use when creating or judging social/comic characters: look for natural charm, an ability to be forgiven for faults, and continuing favour from society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and ritual of a 'Toast' (celebrated beauty)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'toast' is agreed to have a joyous and cheerful import; in modern sense it denotes a celebrated beauty chosen by a company's taste. The inauguration is like balloting (a Doge), marked symbolically with a diamond on a drinking-glass to signify imaginary value and frailty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance for depiction/evaluation: a 'toast' is a social title dependent on company opinion and temporary favour. The object's symbolic trappings (diamond on glass) are used satirically to comment on ephemeral celebrity. Anti-pattern: treating the toast's status as inherent rather than contingent on social approval.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courtship technique: skillful eye-gazing
rubrics_metrics.description: Advice that successful wooing requires 'exquisite judgment' in reading and timing eye-contact: 'to take the language of her eyes to yours exactly, and not let yours talk too fast for hers.' Repetition of significant looks (four or five) leads the lover to a state of pleasurable imagination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Beau Frisk and Lindamira — well-timed looks create vivid mental images and heighten affection. This is prescriptive social technique (timing, moderation, repetition) rather than mere description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patronage/support for new comedies (encouragement policy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Noting a subscription 'made by many persons of wit and quality, for the encouragement of new comedies' as a design that 'will very much contribute to the improvement and diversion of the town,' and a personal lament that tragedies receive less encouragement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: institutional support (subscriptions, patronage) is presented as a criterion for promoting dramatic innovation. The author urges balanced encouragement across genres (comedy and tragedy) to improve theatrical offerings.
